newsitem.title: USA: Spark missing from Clinton's second inaugural. [CORRECTED 18:29 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spark missing from Clinton's second inaugural. [CORRECTED 18:29 GMT]

text.p: A U.S. presidential inaugural is traditionally a glorious festival of national renewal, but Bill Clinton's second swearing-in celebration seems to be missing a certain joyous spark.

There will be splashes of pageantry and non-stop parties as Clinton, at 50 still the youngest president since the late John F. Kennedy, starts another term on Monday. Organisers say it will be the biggest second inaugural in U.S. history.
Still, many in Washington are struck by the subdued atmosphere surrounding the U.S. equivalent of a coronation.

"There's no sense of joyfulness," said longtime Democratic activist Ted Van Dyk. "Here we are with the first Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt to be elected to a second term but there's no joyful mood, just a climate of resignation."

Van Dyk blames partisan rancour stirred by scandals skirling about the trouble-prone Clinton and Newt Gingrich, the brash Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives. This makes for a "poisonous" inaugural backdrop, he said.

Gingrich's ethics problems burst into full bloom at a time when Clinton, already dogged by the Whitewater financial controversy and suspicious re-election fundraising, is fighting to delay a sexual harassment suit against him by a former Arkansas state employee until he leaves office in 2001.

Marlin Fitzwater, press secretary to Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush, shares Van Dyk's view that a withering crossfire between Clinton and Gingrich allies over which is the greater sinner makes the public sceptical about promises of cooperation between the White House and Congress.

"We've lost a lot of hope that we had after the election that there was a chance for meaningful progress," Fitzwater said in an interview. "It's going to take six months to a year of demonstrated ability to work together to convince people that this government can get something done."
Clinton has four top priorities for his second term.

He says he wants to balance the budget, improve education, implement a sweeping new welfare reform law that will require moving two million people from welfare to work and achieve peace in the Middle East, Northern Ireland and Bosnia.
"It's not going to be a very lively, dramatic four years. There's little chance of major new initatives," says Van Dyk.

At an ecumenical prayer breakfast at the White House last week, Clinton, a minority president re-elected on Nov. 5 with 49 percent of the vote, suggested that he sees himself as a kind of catalyst in dealing with the country's problems.
He said a friend had told him, "Don't ever forget that great presidents do not do great things, great presidents get a lot of other people to do great things."

Stephen Hess, a political analyst at Washington's Brookngs Institution, says second-term inaugurals are seldom as exciting as the first ones "when everything is new and all the faces in his administration are new."
But Hess believes Clinton's public image also helps to make this inaugural seem "old hat."

"To some degree, we have just re-elected an unloved president," he said. "Polls show that we approve of Clinton -- the economy is good and the country is at peace -- but the same polls show that we don't trust him very much." he says.

White House officials say Clinton knows he must reinspire the country and will begin with a one-two rhetorical punch, in his inaugural address and a Feb. 4 (corrects from Feb. 6) State of the Union speech.
Shortly thereafter, he plans to travel across the country drumming up support for his agenda, aides say.
